transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... I just can't seem to stop launching projects lately. It's like my brain is just churning out work plans, new certification schedules for my team, completely overhauling my home network... which, by the way, if you ever use the default router your ISP gives you, you're practically begging for a security breach. I was actually explaining this to my neighbor, Dave, just the other night because his Wi-Fi channel was interfering with my new mesh setup. Dave's a good guy, he really is, but he still uses a password he made in 1999 for his dog that died ten years ago. It's wild how little people care about data privacy. 

But anyway, yeah, I've just been doing all that, plus messaging all these old contacts on LinkedIn, trying to get these massive ideas off the ground. And it just gets so intense. I just blow past all the normal limits, you know? I don't even realize I'm doing it until my wife or my director at work has to actually step in and tell me to hit the brakes. Which is why my wife made me come talk to you, honestly.
Have you been experiencing any unusual thoughts, hearing voices, or feeling like people are trying to communicate special messages to you that others might not understand?

Voices? No, no voices. But special messages... yeah, actually. I mean, I pick up on things that other people just completely miss. 

Like at work, even when I’m not in one of those big mood swings where I'm launching a million projects, I still notice these... signs. I'll get completely convinced that certain calendar invites that don't have an agenda attached, or the way someone's Microsoft Teams status suddenly changes to "Do Not Disturb" the second I log on, or just weird passing comments in the hallway... I get convinced they're these coded warnings. Like they are all secretly coordinating and building a case to push me out of the company. 

Which makes zero sense because I literally designed our entire cloud migration strategy. Do you know how hard it is to migrate a legacy on-prem server to AWS without any downtime? It’s a nightmare. My lead engineer, Greg, he wanted to do it over a holiday weekend, which sounds smart until you realize AWS support is on a skeleton crew then. Greg means well, he really does, but he still uses a trackball mouse. I don't know how anyone gets any real work done with a trackball, it just seems so incredibly inefficient. I tried one back in college and my wrist hurt for a week. I actually had to wear a brace during my database management finals... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the messages. But yeah, I just... I get this intense feeling that they're using the very communication systems I set up to secretly plot against me.
Are you still feeling convinced that your coworkers are plotting against you even when you are not in one of those high-energy, project-launching moods?

Yeah, definitely. There have been several stretches, sometimes lasting a few weeks at a time, where I'm just... flat. Not hyped up on projects, not depressed, just totally calm. But even then, I still absolutely believe the Teams statuses are coded warnings. 

Which, speaking of Teams, Microsoft pushed an update last Tuesday that completely messed up the presence indicators across our whole tenant. Half my team was showing as 'Offline' when they were actively pushing code to the repository. I had to write a custom PowerShell script just to force-sync the Azure AD tokens. PowerShell is honestly a lifesaver, though a lot of the younger devs just want to use Python for everything now. I mean, Python is great for data modeling, but for system administration? Come on, you need native OS integration. 

But anyway, yeah, even during those quiet weeks, I know they're plotting. And actually... earlier I said I didn't hear voices. I guess that's not entirely accurate now that I think about it. Because during those same calm stretches, I'll hear these brief comments, like someone saying something right behind my chair, but when I turn around, no one is there. 

I thought maybe it was the HVAC system at first. Our office building has terrible ductwork. They installed these cheap acoustic panels last year that do absolutely nothing to dampen the sound. I told the facilities manager, Linda, that she needed to look into high-density fiberglass, but she just bought whatever was on sale in bulk. Linda's nice, she always brings in donuts on Fridays, but she doesn't understand acoustics at all... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh, right, the moods. Yeah, the warnings and the comments happen even when my mood is completely level.

Aside from the times when you feel high-energy or when you are feeling 'flat' or calm, have you ever experienced periods where you felt deeply sad, hopeless, or lacked the energy to do anything at all?

Yeah, I do. There are definitely times, like... stretches where I just wake up feeling like this completely failed version of myself. Just incredibly heavy and... I don't know, flat isn't even the right word, it's more like being drained of every single drop of motivation. Even just answering my wife's normal, everyday questions feels like it takes a monumental amount of effort. 

It's actually kind of like when a server's CPU usage is maxed out at 99% and it just stops responding to basic ping requests. You know, we had a server do exactly that last month because one of the junior devs wrote an infinite loop in a background processing job. I swear, they don't teach memory management in bootcamps anymore. They just teach them how to string together APIs and call it a day. I had to manually kill the process at 3 AM on a Tuesday. And honestly, waking up at 3 AM is the absolute worst because your circadian rhythm is right in the middle of its deep sleep phase. I read this fascinating article about sleep cycles in a neurobiology journal... they were saying that interrupting REM sleep can actually impair your cognitive function for up to 48 hours. Which explains why I was so irritable the next day when I had to explain to the dev why his code crashed our entire staging environment. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling sad. Yeah, when I get like that, when I'm just so heavy and hopeless, I can barely even look at a computer screen, let alone fix someone else's broken code.
During your life, have you ever experienced these periods of feeling deeply sad and hopeless at the same time that you were also feeling that your coworkers were plotting against you?

At the same time? I'm not really sure. I haven't really kept track of whether they overlap exactly like that. 

Time tracking is actually a huge issue for us right now at work, to be honest. We use Jira for all our sprint planning, and trying to get the developers to log their hours accurately is like pulling teeth. They'll just dump eight hours into a single ticket on Friday afternoon instead of logging it daily as they work. It completely messes up our burndown charts. And if your burndown chart is wrong, you can't accurately predict your velocity for the next sprint. 

I tried implementing this automated time-tracking plugin to make it easier for them, but it integrates directly with our IDEs, and everyone complained it felt like spyware. Which is completely ridiculous, because it's just polling active window titles, it's not keylogging. I know a thing or two about keyloggers, actually. Back when I was a teenager, I accidentally downloaded one from a sketchy gaming forum while trying to get a mod for Half-Life. It took me three days to scrub it out of the Windows registry. The registry is such a convoluted mess, honestly, Microsoft really should have rebuilt it from the ground up when they moved to the NT architecture instead of just patching over it for the last twenty years... 

Wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, the sad periods and the plotting. Yeah, I honestly couldn't tell you if they happen on the exact same days. I just haven't really noticed if they sync up.

When you have these periods where you feel completely 'flat' or calm, and you are not feeling high-energy or deeply sad, do the thoughts about your coworkers plotting against you and the voices you hear continue to happen?

Yeah, they definitely do. Like I mentioned earlier, there have been a few stretches—sometimes lasting a couple of weeks—where my mood is just completely level. Not high-energy, not depressed, just flat. And even during those times, I still absolutely know those Teams statuses are coded warnings, and I still hear those brief comments behind my chair when no one is there. 

It's actually really frustrating when you're trying to concentrate and you hear something, you know? Concentration is so critical when you're managing a team. I was reading this management book the other day—well, listening to the audiobook while I was commuting. The traffic on I-95 has been an absolute nightmare lately because of the construction near exit 42. They've had the right lane closed for three months, and nobody knows how to zipper merge. It's basic traffic flow dynamics! If everyone just used both lanes until the merge point and took turns, it would be so much more efficient. But instead, people get into the left lane two miles early and then try to block anyone who drives up the right lane. It's maddening. I actually started mapping out a traffic simulation model in Python just to prove how inefficient it is. I haven't finished it yet because I keep getting sidetracked by optimizing the rendering engine for the little car graphics...

But yeah, to answer your question, those things—the warnings and the comments—they definitely still happen even when my mood is completely normal and flat for weeks at a time.

Looking back over the years, what is the longest period of time you have experienced these feelings that your coworkers are plotting against you and hearing those voices, without having any significant changes in your mood?

Well, like I was saying, there have definitely been several of those calm or flat stretches... where I wasn't especially up, and I wasn't depressed at all. Just completely level. And some of those stretches lasted a few weeks at a time. But even during those weeks, I still absolutely believed the Teams statuses were coded warnings, and I still heard those brief comments when no one was there. 

It's actually a lot like how a background process keeps running even when the main application window is minimized. You know, we had an issue with that on our mobile app last year. The location services were still polling GPS data in the background even when the user force-closed the app. It was draining people's batteries by like 30% in an hour. We got absolutely roasted in the App Store reviews. People are so brutal in reviews, honestly. It's like they forget there are actual human beings writing the code. I read this sociological study once about the anonymity of the internet and how it completely bypasses the empathy centers of the brain. The researcher was arguing that if we had to attach our real faces and home addresses to every comment, the internet would be a completely different place. Which makes sense, right? Like, you wouldn't walk up to a stranger in a grocery store and scream at them because they bought the last carton of oat milk. Oat milk is actually getting really expensive, by the way. I switched to almond milk for a while, but it takes an insane amount of water to grow almonds. I think it's like a gallon of water per almond or something ridiculous like that. California's aquifers are basically being drained just so we can have dairy alternatives...

But anyway, yeah, the longest period? Probably a few weeks at a time where my mood was just totally flat, but the warnings and the voices were still happening.

Have you ever had a period lasting longer than two weeks where you were experiencing these thoughts about your coworkers and hearing those voices, but you were not feeling either high-energy or deeply sad at all?

Yeah, definitely longer than two weeks. Like I mentioned, there have been several of those calm or flat stretches where I wasn't up, wasn't down, just completely level. And some of those lasted a few weeks at a time. But even during those weeks, I still absolutely knew the Teams statuses were coded warnings, and I still heard those brief comments when no one was there. 

It's strange how things just persist like that, isn't it? Kind of like legacy code. You know, we have this one microservice at work that was written in Perl back in like 2014, and nobody wants to touch it because the original developer left and didn't document anything. It just sits there, doing its thing, and every time we try to migrate it to Node.js, it breaks dependencies we didn't even know existed. Dependencies are the absolute worst part of modern software development. You run `npm install` and suddenly you have 800 megabytes of libraries you don't even understand just to center a div on a webpage. I was reading this article about how fragile the whole open-source ecosystem is. Remember that guy who unpublished his eleven-line string padding module and broke half the internet? It's terrifying when you think about it. Our entire digital infrastructure is basically held together by digital duct tape and the goodwill of some guy in Nebraska maintaining a critical library in his spare time...

But yeah, longer than two weeks? For sure. The mood stays flat, but the warnings and the comments are still there the whole time.

Have you ever experienced these thoughts about your coworkers and the voices during a stretch of time—lasting at least two weeks—where you were not experiencing either the high-energy 'project-launching' periods or the deeply sad, drained periods at all?

Yeah, I know I keep saying this, but yes. Absolutely. There have definitely been several of those calm, flat stretches—definitely lasting at least a couple of weeks at a time—where I wasn't in that crazy project-launching mode, and I wasn't feeling drained or depressed either. Just completely level. But even during those weeks, I still absolutely knew those Teams statuses were coded warnings about me, and I still heard those brief comments behind my chair when no one was there. 

It's funny how you keep asking about the two weeks thing. It reminds me of the sprint cycles we use at work. Agile methodology, you know? Everything is broken down into two-week sprints. Two weeks to plan, code, test, and deploy. Honestly, I think Agile is ruining software development. It forces developers to prioritize speed over quality. You end up with all this technical debt because there's no time to properly architect a solution. We had this one sprint where the product manager—who doesn't know a single thing about coding, by the way—promised the client a fully integrated payment gateway in two weeks. It was a disaster. We had to use this third-party API that had the worst documentation I've ever seen. I mean, it was translated from another language, and half the endpoints just returned generic 500 errors with no payload. I ended up staying awake for three days straight just parsing through their source code on GitHub trying to reverse-engineer how their authentication tokens worked. Coffee stopped working after day two, so I switched to those energy drinks that taste like battery acid. Did you know they put taurine in those? It's an amino acid originally isolated from bull bile. It's wild what we put in our bodies just to meet an arbitrary two-week deadline...

But yes, to answer your question again, yes. At least two weeks. Flat mood, no highs, no lows, but the warnings and the voices were still happening the entire time.
